subtopic_detail: Tubal ectopic pregnancy occurring after previous tubal sterilisation
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 36 year old woman in the early pregnancy assessment unit. She had laparoscopic tubal occlusion three years ago, has missed two periods and a home test was positive last week. For two days she has had a dull ache low on the left side that she rates as three out of ten and settles with paracetamol.

She has had no shoulder tip pain, no dizziness and only light spotting. She lives twenty minutes from the hospital, has a car and can attend for repeat testing. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus with an endometrial thickness of 9 mm, an 18 mm left adnexal mass separate from the ovary with no foetal pole or cardiac activity, and no free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Her full blood count and liver and renal function are all within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78, blood pressure 116/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen with mild left iliac fossa tenderness, no guarding, no cervical excitation
data_table.Investigations: Beta human chorionic gonadotrophin 1450 IU/L; transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus with an 18 mm left adnexal mass, no cardiac activity and no free fluid; full blood count, liver and renal function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give single dose intramuscular methotrexate with serial hCG monitoring
options.rationale: She meets every criterion for medical management with a level well below 5000 IU/L, a mass under 35 mm, no cardiac activity, no significant pain, no haemoperitoneum and reliable access for follow up (Source: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy; Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy
Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Perform laparoscopic salpingectomy of the affected left tube today
options.rationale: Surgery is indicated for haemodynamic instability, significant pain, a mass above 35 mm, cardiac activity, a level above 5000 IU/L or failed medical therapy, none of which applies here (Source: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.text: Perform laparoscopic salpingostomy to preserve the tubal patency
options.rationale: Salpingostomy is chosen over salpingectomy only when the contralateral tube is absent or damaged and future fertility depends on that tube, and it leaves a risk of persistent trophoblast (Source: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.text: Repeat the hCG in 48 hours and rescan once it exceeds 2000 IU/L
options.rationale: The discriminatory zone applies to a pregnancy of unknown location, and once an adnexal mass separate from the ovary is visualised with an empty uterus the diagnosis is already made (Source: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.text: Manage her expectantly with weekly hCG until the level falls to zero
options.rationale: Expectant management is limited to a low and already falling level in a minimally symptomatic woman, and her level of 1450 IU/L with ongoing pain does not fit that group (Source: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

explanation.summary: Pregnancy after tubal sterilisation is uncommon but carries a disproportionately high probability of being ectopic, because the occluded tube can recanalise or form a fistula that admits sperm while obstructing the passage of an embryo. Methotrexate is given as a single intramuscular dose calculated on body surface area, with human chorionic gonadotrophin measured on days 4 and 7 and a fall of at least fifteen per cent between those days indicating success. Around fifteen per cent of women need a second dose and a smaller proportion still proceed to surgery, so counselling must set expectations for weeks of follow up. Women must avoid alcohol, non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs, folate supplements and conception for at least three months after treatment.
key_points: Pregnancy after tubal sterilisation has a high probability of being ectopic
Medical management requires hCG below 5000 IU/L, mass under 35 mm and no cardiac activity
Reliable follow up is a formal criterion, not an optional extra
Success is judged by a fall of at least fifteen per cent between days 4 and 7
Salpingectomy is preferred over salpingostomy when the other tube is healthy
explanation.pearls: Human chorionic gonadotrophin commonly rises between day 1 and day 4 after methotrexate, so an increase at day 4 is expected and is not treatment failure, which is judged on the day 4 to day 7 comparison.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Mixed incontinence with impaired bladder emptying before continence surgery
stem:
You are the urogynaecology registrar seeing a 62 year old woman who leaks both when she coughs and when she cannot reach the toilet in time, and who says the urgency episodes bother her far more. She has been referred with a request to consider a sling.

She reports a slow stream, has to sit for a while before anything comes and feels she has not finished afterwards. She has no prolapse below the hymen and her urinalysis is clear with no growth on culture. Her post void residual volume measured twice is 180 mL and 210 mL. Urodynamic testing shows detrusor overactivity with leakage during filling, urodynamic stress incontinence on coughing, and a low pressure poorly sustained detrusor contraction on voiding.

data_table.Examination: No prolapse beyond the hymen, weak but present pelvic floor contraction, no palpable bladder after voiding
data_table.Investigations: Post void residual 180 mL and 210 mL on two occasions; urodynamics show detrusor overactivity, urodynamic stress incontinence and impaired detrusor contractility; urine culture no growth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Proceed to a midurethral sling to address the stress component now
options.rationale: Placing a sling in a woman who already empties poorly risks frank retention needing self catheterisation or tape division, and it would not help the urgency that troubles her most (Source: RANZCOG: Urinary Incontinence in Women).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Urinary Incontinence in Women

options.text: Start solifenacin now to control the urgency before any surgery
options.rationale: Antimuscarinic therapy reduces detrusor contractility further and would be expected to increase a residual already above 180 mL (Source: RANZCOG: Urinary Incontinence in Women; Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Urinary Incontinence in Women
Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Start bladder retraining and defer surgery until emptying improves
options.rationale: Conservative therapy with timed voiding, double voiding and pelvic floor work addresses the dominant urgency symptom without worsening emptying, and the residual must fall before any obstructive procedure is contemplated (Source: RANZCOG: Urinary Incontinence in Women).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Urinary Incontinence in Women

options.text: Inject intradetrusor botulinum toxin A at the next available list
options.rationale: Botulinum toxin causes clinically significant retention in a substantial minority even with normal baseline emptying, and consent requires willingness to self catheterise (Source: RANZCOG: Urinary Incontinence in Women).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Urinary Incontinence in Women

options.text: Refer for sacral neuromodulation assessment as the first treatment
options.rationale: Neuromodulation is a third line therapy considered only after conservative measures and pharmacotherapy have been tried, although it does have the advantage of treating both overactivity and non obstructive retention (Source: RANZCOG: Urinary Incontinence in Women).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Urinary Incontinence in Women

explanation.summary: Mixed urinary incontinence is treated by identifying which component bothers the woman most and starting there, because the two components respond to different interventions. This case is one of the clear indications for urodynamics, since the coexisting voiding difficulty changes the safety profile of everything that follows. Impaired detrusor contractility with a raised residual makes both antimuscarinic therapy and any obstructive procedure hazardous, so conservative management comes first and the residual is rechecked. Beta 3 agonists such as mirabegron are often preferred over antimuscarinics in this situation because they relax the detrusor during filling without impairing the voiding contraction to the same degree.
key_points: Treat the component of mixed incontinence that troubles the woman most
Voiding dysfunction is a firm indication for urodynamic testing
A raised post void residual makes antimuscarinics and slings hazardous
Conservative therapy with timed and double voiding precedes any procedure
Botulinum toxin requires willingness to perform intermittent self catheterisation
explanation.pearls: Mirabegron is the preferred pharmacological choice when detrusor contractility is impaired, but it must be avoided in uncontrolled hypertension and blood pressure should be checked before starting and after a month.

subtopic_detail: Hoarding disorder distinguished from obsessive compulsive disorder
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 58 year old man referred after a council fire safety inspection found his home filled to shoulder height with newspapers, containers and unopened mail, leaving only narrow paths between rooms. He has lived alone since his mother died twelve years ago.

He tells you the items will be useful one day and becomes visibly distressed when you ask what would happen if a skip were brought in. He describes no fear of contamination, no repeated washing or checking, and no intrusive thoughts that he tries to neutralise. His mood is reactive and he sleeps and eats normally. His score on a cognitive screening test is 29 out of 30 and there is no history of stroke or head injury.

data_table.Examination: Well groomed, no psychomotor change, no thought disorder, insight limited into the extent of the risk
data_table.Investigations: Cognitive screening 29 out of 30; full blood count, electrolytes, thyroid function and B12 within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Start fluvoxamine at a high dose as used for compulsive disorder
options.rationale: Serotonergic antidepressants have far weaker evidence in hoarding than in obsessive compulsive disorder, and they are considered after or alongside psychological therapy rather than as the first step (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders

options.text: Arrange a compulsory house clearance through the local council now
options.rationale: Forced clearance without treatment reliably produces severe distress and rapid re accumulation, and it damages the therapeutic relationship needed for any lasting change (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders

options.text: Apply to the tribunal for a financial administration order for him
options.rationale: Substitute decision making requires demonstrated impairment of decision making capacity, and an intact cognitive screen with a clear account of his reasoning does not establish that (Source: Australian guardianship and administration frameworks).
source_refs: Australian guardianship and administration frameworks

options.text: Refer for hoarding specific cognitive behavioural therapy for him
options.rationale: Structured cognitive behavioural therapy adapted for hoarding, addressing acquiring, sorting decisions and beliefs about possessions with in home practice, has the strongest evidence for this disorder (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders

options.text: Start risperidone at a low dose to address the poor insight shown
options.rationale: His beliefs are overvalued rather than delusional and antipsychotics have no established role, while adding metabolic and extrapyramidal risk (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

explanation.summary: Hoarding disorder was separated from obsessive compulsive disorder because its phenomenology, course and treatment response all differ, and the distinction matters clinically rather than academically. The core is persistent difficulty discarding possessions because of a perceived need to save them, with distress at discarding and clutter that prevents the intended use of living areas. Unlike obsessive compulsive disorder, the saving is not driven by intrusive thoughts and the behaviour is often experienced as reasonable rather than unwanted. Treatment is predominantly psychological, and the risks that bring these patients to attention are fire, falls, infestation and eviction, so working with fire services and housing alongside the therapy is part of the plan.
key_points: Hoarding disorder is a distinct diagnosis, not a subtype of obsessive compulsive disorder
Saving is driven by perceived future usefulness rather than by intrusive thoughts
Beliefs are typically overvalued rather than delusional
Hoarding specific cognitive behavioural therapy is the first line treatment
Forced clearance without therapy leads to re accumulation and distress
explanation.pearls: New onset hoarding after the age of 50 with no lifelong pattern should prompt cognitive assessment and neuroimaging, because behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia and orbitofrontal lesions can present this way.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders

subtopic_detail: Management threshold for a tic disorder in a school aged child
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 9 year old boy whose parents are worried about movements that started about eighteen months ago. He blinks hard and shrugs one shoulder, and for the past six months he has also made a repeated throat clearing sound.

His parents say the movements come and go in waves, are worse when he is tired or excited, and disappear when he is absorbed in building models. He can hold them back briefly at school but says the urge builds until he has to let go. He is doing well academically, has friends, and denies any low mood, although two boys in another class have started imitating the sounds. He has no repetitive rituals, no compulsions and no difficulty concentrating in class.

data_table.Examination: Observed eye blinking, unilateral shoulder shrug and throat clearing, suppressible on request, normal neurological examination

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start low dose risperidone and monitor his weight and prolactin
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are reserved for tics causing pain, injury or substantial functional impairment, and their metabolic and extrapyramidal burden is not justified in a child functioning well (Source: RANZCP guidance on tic disorders; Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: RANZCP guidance on tic disorders
Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Provide psychoeducation and refer for behavioural tic therapy for him
options.rationale: Comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics, combining habit reversal with function based strategies, is the recommended first line treatment and pairs with education for the family and the school (Source: RANZCP guidance on tic disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP guidance on tic disorders

options.text: Start clonidine at night and review the tics again in four weeks
options.rationale: Clonidine is a reasonable pharmacological choice particularly where attention symptoms coexist, but medication follows a trial of behavioural therapy when tics are not causing impairment (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Arrange an electroencephalogram to exclude a seizure disorder in him
options.rationale: Tics are suppressible, preceded by a premonitory urge and change over time, which distinguishes them from seizures and makes electrophysiological testing unnecessary (Source: RCH CPG: Tics).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Tics

options.text: Refer for botulinum toxin injection into the affected muscle groups
options.rationale: Botulinum toxin has a narrow role in a severe focal tic causing pain or injury, such as a violent neck tic, and is not used for generalised mild tics (Source: RANZCP guidance on tic disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP guidance on tic disorders

explanation.summary: Tic disorders affect around one in a hundred school aged children and Tourette disorder is diagnosed when multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic have been present for more than a year. The natural history is the most important thing to convey, because tics typically peak between 10 and 12 years and then improve substantially through adolescence in most children. Treatment is directed at impairment rather than at the tics themselves, so a child who is learning, socialising and not in pain needs education and school liaison rather than medication. Coexisting attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and obsessive compulsive disorder are present in a majority and often cause more impairment than the tics, so they must be sought at every review.
key_points: Tourette disorder requires multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic for over a year
A premonitory urge with brief suppressibility distinguishes tics from other movements
Tics usually peak around 10 to 12 years and improve through adolescence
Treat impairment rather than the presence of tics
Screen for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and obsessive compulsive disorder at every review
explanation.pearls: If medication becomes necessary, clonidine is often chosen first in Australian practice because it treats coexisting attention symptoms, whereas risperidone and aripiprazole are more effective for the tics but bring weight gain and prolactin elevation.

subtopic_detail: First line treatment for binge eating disorder in adulthood
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34 year old woman who describes eating enormous amounts in the evening after her children are asleep, getting through a family sized block of chocolate and several packets of biscuits within two hours. She says she cannot stop once she starts and feels disgusted with herself afterwards.

This has happened about three times a week for eight months and she hides the wrappers from her partner. She does not make herself vomit, does not use laxatives or diuretics, does not fast between episodes and exercises only by walking the dog. Her body mass index is 34 kg/m2 and her weight has risen 9 kg over the year. Her mood is low only in the hours after an episode and she has no thoughts of self harm.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 34 kg/m2, no parotid swelling, no dental erosion, no Russell sign on the knuckles
data_table.Investigations: Electrolytes, full blood count, thyroid function and fasting glucose within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Start lisdexamfetamine as the initial treatment for the binge episodes
options.rationale: Pharmacotherapy can reduce binge frequency but is positioned after or alongside structured psychological therapy rather than instead of it, and it does not address the maintaining cognitions (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Eating Disorders; Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Eating Disorders
Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Refer for bariatric surgery assessment given her current body weight
options.rationale: Untreated binge eating is a relative contraindication to bariatric surgery because unaddressed loss of control eating predicts poorer weight outcomes and postoperative complications (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Eating Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Eating Disorders

options.text: Start fluoxetine 60 mg daily as the sole initial treatment for her
options.rationale: High dose fluoxetine is the established pharmacological choice for bulimia nervosa, and while antidepressants have some effect here they are not the first line intervention (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Eating Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Eating Disorders

options.text: Refer to a dietitian for a structured energy restricted weight loss diet
options.rationale: Dietary restriction is a well recognised trigger for further binge episodes, so weight focused restriction without psychological treatment tends to worsen the disorder (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Eating Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Eating Disorders

options.text: Refer for eating disorder focused cognitive behavioural therapy for her
options.rationale: Enhanced cognitive behavioural therapy targeting the binge cycle, regular eating and the overvaluation of shape and weight produces the highest remission rates and is the recommended first line treatment (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Eating Disorders; NEDC Australian treatment principles).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Eating Disorders
NEDC Australian treatment principles

explanation.summary: Binge eating disorder is the most common eating disorder in Australia and is defined by recurrent objectively large binges with loss of control and marked distress, in the absence of the compensatory behaviours that define bulimia nervosa. It is frequently missed because clinicians focus on the weight rather than asking directly about loss of control, secrecy and shame around eating. Structured psychological therapy is first line, and it works by establishing a pattern of regular eating that removes the restriction driving the binges, then addressing the beliefs about shape and weight. Australian general practitioners can access an eating disorder treatment plan providing subsidised psychological and dietetic sessions, which is worth arranging at the first consultation.
key_points: Binge eating disorder has no regular compensatory behaviours
Ask directly about loss of control, secrecy and shame rather than about weight
Enhanced cognitive behavioural therapy is the first line treatment
Energy restricted dieting can precipitate further binge episodes
An eating disorder treatment plan gives access to subsidised sessions in Australia
explanation.pearls: Absence of parotid enlargement, dental erosion and callusing over the knuckles helps confirm that no purging is occurring, which is the single distinction between binge eating disorder and bulimia nervosa.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Eating Disorders

subtopic_detail: Body dysmorphic disorder presenting as a request for cosmetic surgery
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 23 year old man who asks for a referral to a surgeon to have his nose reshaped. He says it is crooked and takes up his whole face, and that people stare at it on the train.

He checks his profile in reflective surfaces for about four hours a day, angles his head in conversation to hide one side, and has stopped going to gatherings where photographs might be taken. He has already had a septorhinoplasty and a chin filler elsewhere, and says neither made any difference. He describes his appearance as ruining his life but sleeps and eats normally, enjoys his job and has no anhedonia or thoughts of self harm. His nose appears entirely unremarkable to you.

data_table.Examination: Nose of normal appearance with no deformity, no skin excoriation, mood euthymic with reactive affect

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer to a plastic surgeon for an independent second opinion for him
options.rationale: Further cosmetic procedures in this disorder rarely satisfy the patient and commonly shift the preoccupation to another feature, as his two previous procedures already demonstrate (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders

options.text: Start olanzapine at a low dose to address the fixed belief he holds
options.rationale: Even delusional intensity beliefs in this disorder respond to serotonergic and psychological treatment rather than to antipsychotic monotherapy, which is used only as augmentation (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy rather than to a surgeon
options.rationale: Cognitive behavioural therapy tailored to this disorder, with exposure and response prevention targeting mirror checking and camouflaging, is the first line treatment and addresses the mechanism the surgery cannot reach (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders

options.text: Arrange a psychology referral for social anxiety focused therapy for him
options.rationale: Social avoidance here is secondary to appearance preoccupation rather than to fear of negative evaluation in general, so generic social anxiety therapy misses the target (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders

options.text: Start a low dose of sertraline and review him again in six months
options.rationale: Serotonergic antidepressants do help but require higher doses than in depression and a trial of at least twelve weeks, and a six month review without therapy leaves him untreated meanwhile (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

explanation.summary: Body dysmorphic disorder is a preoccupation with a perceived defect that is unobservable or slight to others, accompanied by repetitive behaviours such as mirror checking, camouflaging, reassurance seeking and comparison. It presents to cosmetic and dermatology services far more often than to psychiatry, and prevalence in cosmetic surgery populations is around ten per cent compared with two per cent in the community. Insight is frequently poor or absent, which is why the diagnosis is defined by the behaviour and the discrepancy with observers rather than by whether the patient agrees. Suicide risk is high in this population, considerably above that seen in obsessive compulsive disorder, so risk assessment is mandatory even when mood appears reactive.
key_points: The defect is unobservable or slight to others and accompanied by repetitive behaviours
Prevalence in cosmetic surgery populations approaches ten per cent
Cosmetic procedures rarely satisfy and preoccupation often shifts elsewhere
Cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and response prevention is first line
Suicide risk is high and must be assessed at every contact
explanation.pearls: Serotonergic antidepressants for this disorder require doses at the upper end of the range, such as fluoxetine up to 60 to 80 mg daily, and a trial of at least twelve weeks before response is judged.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders

subtopic_detail: New behaviour change in a non verbal adult with intellectual disability
stem:
You are the general practitioner asked to visit a group home for a 24 year old man with moderate intellectual disability who communicates with gestures and a small set of signs. Over the past three weeks he has begun hitting the side of his head with his palm and shouting, sometimes for an hour at a time, and staff have requested something to settle him.

Staffing, housemates and his weekly routine are unchanged, and his family visits as usual. He has been leaving most of his dinner, has lost 2 kg, and staff have noticed him holding his right cheek and pulling at that ear. He last saw a dentist four years ago. He takes no regular medication and his bowels have been opening normally.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92, blood pressure 122/76, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 37.2
data_table.Examination: Guards the right side of his face on approach, will not allow full oral examination, no external ear discharge, chest and abdomen unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Weight down 2 kg over three weeks, no investigations performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Examine for an untreated physical cause including dental disease
options.rationale: New behaviour change in a person who cannot report symptoms is treated as pain or illness until proven otherwise, and localising signs with reduced intake and weight loss point directly to a dental or ear source needing examination, sometimes under sedation (Source: RANZCP guidance on the mental health of people with intellectual disability).
source_refs: RANZCP guidance on the mental health of people with intellectual disability

options.text: Start regular low dose risperidone and review him again in four weeks
options.rationale: Prescribing psychotropics for behaviour without a psychiatric diagnosis is the practice that national reviews have specifically targeted for reduction, and it would mask an untreated painful condition (Source: RANZCP guidance on the mental health of people with intellectual disability).
source_refs: RANZCP guidance on the mental health of people with intellectual disability

options.text: Prescribe as needed diazepam for staff to give when he is agitated
options.rationale: As needed sedation carries falls, aspiration and disinhibition risk and would obscure the pattern of the behaviour that is the main diagnostic clue (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Admit him to the acute psychiatric inpatient unit for observation
options.rationale: An unfamiliar noisy environment typically escalates distress in this population and there is no psychiatric indication established, so admission should follow rather than replace a medical assessment (Source: RANZCP guidance on the mental health of people with intellectual disability).
source_refs: RANZCP guidance on the mental health of people with intellectual disability

options.text: Ask the service to write a positive behaviour support plan for him
options.rationale: A behaviour support plan is a valuable part of ongoing care but is built on a formal functional assessment that must first exclude a medical driver of the behaviour (Source: NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission behaviour support guidance).
source_refs: NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission behaviour support guidance

explanation.summary: People with intellectual disability experience the same physical illnesses as everyone else but often cannot describe them, so pain and illness are expressed as changed behaviour. Diagnostic overshadowing describes the systematic error of attributing new symptoms to the disability itself rather than investigating them, and it contributes to the substantially shorter life expectancy in this population. Dental disease, constipation, gastro oesophageal reflux, otitis media, urinary infection and fractures are the classic missed causes, and a physical assessment sometimes requires sedation or general anaesthesia to complete. Psychotropic medication prescribed for behaviour without a psychiatric diagnosis meets the definition of chemical restraint under Australian disability regulation and must be reported and reviewed.
key_points: New behaviour change in a non verbal person means look for pain or illness first
Diagnostic overshadowing is a leading cause of avoidable harm in this group
Dental disease, constipation, reflux and ear infection are the classic missed causes
Psychotropics given for behaviour without a diagnosis constitute chemical restraint
Functional behaviour assessment follows exclusion of medical causes
explanation.pearls: Examination under general anaesthesia combined with a dental review is a legitimate and often necessary investigation in this population, and arranging both in a single anaesthetic avoids repeated distressing attempts at bedside examination.

sources.label: RANZCP guidance on the mental health of people with intellectual disability
NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission behaviour support guidance

subtopic_detail: Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia presenting as late onset mood change
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 58 year old accountant brought in by his wife, who says he is not the man she married. Over eighteen months he has spent nearly forty thousand dollars on equipment he has never used, has begun making blunt remarks about strangers' weight in the supermarket, and no longer seems to notice when she is upset.

He now eats two packets of sweet biscuits a day when he never had a sweet tooth, and he sits in the same chair for hours unless prompted. He sleeps soundly through the night, wakes at his usual hour and denies feeling sad. He has no personal or family history of mood disorder and takes no medication. His recall of three items at five minutes is intact and his score on a cognitive screening test is 28 out of 30, with difficulty only on a verbal fluency task.

data_table.Examination: No focal neurological deficit, no tremor or rigidity, affect fatuous with reduced concern about the consultation
data_table.Investigations: Cognitive screening 28 out of 30 with reduced verbal fluency and intact delayed recall; full blood count, electrolytes, liver function, thyroid function, B12 and folate within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start sertraline for a late onset depressive episode and review him
options.rationale: He has no sadness, no sleep disturbance and no diurnal variation, and the apathy here is a loss of initiation rather than low mood, so antidepressant therapy treats the wrong syndrome (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders

options.text: Start quetiapine for a first manic episode occurring at this age
options.rationale: Mania requires elevated or irritable mood with reduced need for sleep and increased energy, and his sleep is normal while his activity is reduced rather than increased (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders

options.text: Repeat cognitive screening in six months before making any referral
options.rationale: Brief cognitive screens are insensitive to frontal pathology because memory and orientation are preserved, so repeating one would give false reassurance for another six months (Source: Dementia Australia clinical guidance).
source_refs: Dementia Australia clinical guidance

options.text: Refer for psychology to address the recent stress in his marriage
options.rationale: The marital strain is a consequence of the behavioural change rather than its cause, and framing it as a relationship problem delays the diagnosis (Source: Dementia Australia clinical guidance).
source_refs: Dementia Australia clinical guidance

options.text: Arrange neuroimaging and refer to a cognitive disorders clinic
options.rationale: Progressive disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy and altered eating with preserved memory in a man under 65 describe the behavioural variant syndrome, and structural imaging with specialist assessment is the pathway to diagnosis (Source: Dementia Australia clinical guidance; RANZCP guidance on assessment of cognitive impairment).
source_refs: Dementia Australia clinical guidance
RANZCP guidance on assessment of cognitive impairment

explanation.summary: Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia is the commonest young onset dementia after Alzheimer disease and is regularly misdiagnosed as depression, bipolar disorder or a midlife crisis for years before the true nature becomes clear. The diagnostic features are early behavioural disinhibition, apathy, loss of sympathy and empathy, perseverative or compulsive behaviour, hyperorality with a shift toward sweet foods, and an executive predominant cognitive profile with relative sparing of memory. Standard bedside screens perform poorly because they weight orientation and recall heavily, so a normal score is not reassuring and verbal fluency is often the only abnormality. Diagnosis matters for the family well beyond prognosis, since it reframes hurtful behaviour as illness and opens access to disability and carer support.
key_points: Behavioural variant disease presents with personality change and preserved memory
Hyperorality with a new preference for sweet foods is highly characteristic
Brief cognitive screens are insensitive because they weight memory and orientation
Apathy in this syndrome is loss of initiation rather than low mood
Young onset presentation requires structural imaging and specialist assessment
explanation.pearls: Absence of the biological features of depression, with sound sleep, preserved appetite for sweet foods and no diurnal mood variation, is the clinical hinge that separates frontal apathy from a late onset depressive episode.

sources.label: RANZCP guidance on assessment of cognitive impairment
RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders

subtopic_detail: Psychosis persisting a month after abstinence from methamphetamine
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar planning discharge for a 22 year old man admitted four weeks ago. He arrived believing his housemates were filming him for a syndicate and hearing two voices discussing him in the third person, after three months of using crystal methamphetamine several times a week.

His urine drug screen was positive on admission and has been negative on weekly testing since, and the ward is a locked unit with no access to substances. He was started on olanzapine 10 mg at night and his agitation settled within days, but he still believes the filming occurred and still hears the voices most days. He has no blunting of affect, no social withdrawal and remains motivated to return to his apprenticeship. His mood is euthymic with no manic or depressive features.

data_table.Examination: Persecutory delusion of being filmed held with full conviction, third person auditory hallucinations most days, no negative symptoms, no thought disorder
data_table.Investigations: Weekly urine drug screens negative for four weeks; full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits; computed tomography of the brain normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan on discharge?

options.text: Stop the antipsychotic at discharge as the drug screen is now clear
options.rationale: A negative screen confirms abstinence but symptoms have persisted for a month beyond it, and stopping treatment now risks relapse of an unresolved psychotic illness (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Schizophrenia and Related Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Schizophrenia and Related Disorders

options.text: Continue the antipsychotic and refer to an early psychosis service
options.rationale: Psychosis persisting well beyond the expected resolution of intoxication and withdrawal is no longer adequately explained as substance induced, so treatment continues with specialist follow up that can revise the diagnosis over time (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Schizophrenia and Related Disorders; Orygen early psychosis clinical guidance).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Schizophrenia and Related Disorders
Orygen early psychosis clinical guidance

options.text: Switch him to clozapine because of the incomplete symptom response
options.rationale: Treatment resistance requires failure of two adequate antipsychotic trials of at least six weeks each at therapeutic dose, and he has had one drug for four weeks (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Schizophrenia and Related Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Schizophrenia and Related Disorders

options.text: Reduce and cease the antipsychotic over the next fortnight after discharge
options.rationale: A planned taper is reasonable once symptoms have fully remitted and a period of stability has passed, and neither condition is met while the delusion is held with full conviction (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Schizophrenia and Related Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Schizophrenia and Related Disorders

options.text: Add sodium valproate for mood stabilisation before he is discharged
options.rationale: A mood stabiliser is indicated when an affective syndrome is present, and his mood has been euthymic throughout without manic or depressive features (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

explanation.summary: Substance induced psychotic disorder and a primary psychotic illness precipitated by substance use look identical at presentation, and time is the only reliable discriminator. Methamphetamine induced psychosis typically resolves within days to a few weeks of abstinence, so symptoms persisting at a month in a controlled environment shift the diagnosis toward a primary psychotic disorder. Longitudinal studies show that around a quarter to a third of people diagnosed with methamphetamine induced psychosis are later diagnosed with schizophrenia, and continued use is the strongest predictor of that transition. The practical consequence is that treatment continues and follow up is arranged with a service that can review the diagnosis rather than discharging on the basis of a clean urine screen.
key_points: Substance induced psychosis usually resolves within days to weeks of abstinence
Persistence beyond a month of documented abstinence points to a primary disorder
A negative urine screen confirms abstinence, not diagnosis
Treatment resistance requires two adequate trials of at least six weeks each
A substantial minority later receive a schizophrenia diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Ongoing methamphetamine use is the single strongest predictor of conversion from substance induced psychosis to a schizophrenia diagnosis, so relapse prevention work is as much a psychosis intervention as the antipsychotic itself.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Schizophrenia and Related Disorders

subtopic_detail: Eligibility screening before ketamine treatment for resistant depression
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a mood disorders clinic seeing a 44 year old woman with a nine year history of recurrent major depression. She has completed adequate trials of sertraline, venlafaxine and mirtazapine at therapeutic doses for at least eight weeks each, plus quetiapine augmentation, with only partial benefit and a current score in the severe range.

She has no psychotic symptoms, no history of mania and no current substance use. She has read about ketamine and asks whether she can start it. She has never seen a doctor about her blood pressure and takes no antihypertensive. Her blood pressure today is 168 over 104, repeated after ten minutes seated at 166 over 102, and a reading taken at her pharmacy last month was similar.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84, blood pressure 168/104 repeated at 166/102, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 29 kg/m2, no cardiac murmur, no papilloedema, no focal neurological signs
data_table.Investigations: Electrolytes, liver function, thyroid function and full blood count within normal limits; electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm with voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start esketamine nasal spray at the next available clinic appointment
options.rationale: Ketamine and esketamine produce a transient rise in blood pressure peaking about forty minutes after dosing, so starting treatment with uncontrolled hypertension risks a hypertensive emergency (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook; RANZCP guidance on ketamine for depression).
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook
RANZCP guidance on ketamine for depression

options.text: Refer for electroconvulsive therapy as the only remaining option for her
options.rationale: Electroconvulsive therapy is an effective option in treatment resistant depression, but it is not the only one remaining and presenting it that way forecloses a reasonable discussion (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders

options.text: Add lithium augmentation and review her response again in six weeks
options.rationale: Lithium augmentation is a well evidenced next step and may well feature in her plan, but it does not address the finding that requires action before any ketamine treatment (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders

options.text: Control the blood pressure before considering any ketamine therapy
options.rationale: Uncontrolled hypertension is a specific contraindication to ketamine and esketamine, so her newly identified stage 2 hypertension with electrocardiographic left ventricular hypertrophy must be investigated and treated first (Source: RANZCP guidance on ketamine for depression; Heart Foundation Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Hypertension).
source_refs: RANZCP guidance on ketamine for depression
Heart Foundation Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Hypertension

options.text: Refer for transcranial magnetic stimulation instead of ketamine therapy
options.rationale: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation is a legitimate alternative with no haemodynamic contraindication, but substituting it leaves an unmanaged cardiovascular risk that needs attention in its own right (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders

explanation.summary: Ketamine and its S enantiomer esketamine have rapid antidepressant effects in treatment resistant depression, and Australian services deliver them under supervised protocols with post dose observation. Both reliably raise blood pressure and heart rate for one to two hours after administration, which is why uncontrolled hypertension, aneurysmal vascular disease and recent cardiovascular events are contraindications. Screening also excludes a history of psychosis or mania, current substance use disorder involving ketamine, and pregnancy, and it must include a plan for the dissociation and sedation that follow each dose. Depression is itself a cardiovascular risk factor, so identifying untreated hypertension in this clinic is a meaningful intervention regardless of which antidepressant strategy follows.
key_points: Ketamine raises blood pressure transiently for one to two hours after dosing
Uncontrolled hypertension and aneurysmal disease are contraindications
Screening also covers psychosis, mania, substance use and pregnancy
Treatment resistance means failure of two or more adequate trials
Depression itself carries excess cardiovascular risk warranting active management
explanation.pearls: Blood pressure peaks around forty minutes after esketamine and returns to baseline by about two hours, which is why protocols require observation for at least two hours with monitoring rather than discharge once dissociation resolves.

sources.label: RANZCP guidance on ketamine for depression
Heart Foundation Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Hypertension
RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders
